{
"Service-Oriented Architecture": "An architectural style that structures software systems as a collection of loosely coupled, independently deployable services communicating through well-defined contracts. It promotes reusability, interoperability, and flexibility by decomposing functionality into discrete service units.",
"Service": "A self-contained, independently deployable software component that exposes specific functionality through a well-defined contract and interface. Services are the fundamental building blocks of a service-oriented architecture.",
"Contract": "A formal specification that defines the obligations, expectations, and terms of interaction between a service and its consumers. It typically describes the service's interface, functionality, inputs, outputs, and quality attributes.",
"Interface": "The technical boundary through which a service exposes its operations and is accessed by consumers. It defines the signatures, protocols, and data formats required to invoke the service's functionality.",
"Functionality": "The specific business or technical capability that a service provides to its consumers. It represents the useful work performed when the service's operations are invoked.",
"Composition": "The process of combining multiple services to create higher-level functionality or fulfill complex business requirements. It enables reuse of existing services to build new capabilities without duplicating logic.",
"Business Process": "A structured sequence of activities and tasks performed to achieve a specific business goal or outcome. In SOA, business processes are often realized by composing and coordinating multiple services.",
"Orchestration": "A centralized coordination approach in which a controlling component directs the execution and interaction of multiple services according to a defined workflow. It provides explicit control over service invocation order and data flow.",
"Workflow": "A defined sequence of steps, decisions, and service invocations that describes how work progresses to accomplish a specific process or goal. Workflows are used by orchestrators to coordinate service execution.",
"Governance": "The set of policies, processes, and controls that guide the design, deployment, and lifecycle management of services within an organization. It ensures consistency, compliance, and alignment with business objectives.",
"Service Versioning": "The practice of managing changes to service contracts and implementations over time while maintaining compatibility with existing consumers. It enables services to evolve without disrupting dependent systems.",
"Quality": "The set of non-functional characteristics of a service, such as reliability, performance, security, and availability. Quality attributes are typically monitored and enforced through governance.",
"Loose Coupling": "A design principle in which services have minimal dependencies on one another's internal implementations, interacting only through their contracts. It enables independent evolution, replacement, and scaling of services.",
"Independent Deployability": "The property that allows a service to be built, updated, and released without requiring simultaneous changes or redeployment of other services. It supports agility, continuous delivery, and fault isolation.",
"System": "An organized collection of interacting components, such as services, that together deliver cohesive functionality to fulfill business or technical objectives. In SOA, a system is realized through the composition and coordination of services."
}
